items.prompt: Which word is spelled correctly?

options.why: The /j/ sound after a short vowel is spelled dge.
The word needs a silent e at the end.
The letter j is not used for this sound at the end of a word.

hints: The word ends with the /j/ sound after a short vowel.
After a short vowel we write dge.
Remember: badge, fridge, bridge.
items.explanation: After a short vowel the /j/ sound is spelled dge, so the word is bridge.

items.prompt: Sort each word by how the /k/ sound is spelled.
hints: Look at the letters that make the /k/ sound.
Short words that end in /k/ after a short vowel often use ck.
Que is usually found at the end of words borrowed from French.
items.explanation: Duck and stick use ck, unique and antique end in que, and chorus and echo use ch for the /k/ sound.

items.prompt: Listen and spell the word.
items.sentence: Wulan stirred the fudge slowly in the pan.
hints: It ends with the /j/ sound.
The sound comes right after a short vowel.
Think of badge and edge: f-u-d-...
items.explanation: After the short vowel u, the /j/ sound is spelled dge. The word is fudge.

items.prompt: Which rule explains why match has tch but torch has only ch?

options.text: Tch comes straight after a short vowel, and ch comes after a consonant or long vowel
Tch is always used at the end of a word
options.why: Not always: many words end in ch, such as bench and teach.

options.text: Ch is used only in words from French
options.why: The rule is about sounds, not French words.

options.text: Tch is used only for nouns
options.why: Verbs such as catch also use tch.

hints: Look at the sound before the ending.
In match the vowel is short. In torch, an r comes before ch.
Short vowel then tch.
items.explanation: After a short vowel we write tch (match, catch). After a consonant or a long vowel we write ch (torch, teach).

items.prompt: Sort each word by the way it ends.
hints: Check the sound before the ending.
After a short vowel, we usually use tch. After a long vowel or a consonant, use ch.
Start with pitch: is the i short?
items.explanation: Pitch, switch, catch and stretch have a short vowel before the sound. Beach, bench, coach and lunch do not.

items.prompt: Complete the word with ge or dge. The fri___ was full of cold juice.
hints: The /j/ sound comes after a short vowel.
Short vowel means dge.
Say the word: fri-j. Is the i short or long?
items.explanation: The i in fridge is a short vowel, so the /j/ sound is spelled dge.

items.prompt: Complete the word with ge or dge. Please turn to the next pa___ in your book.
hints: The /j/ sound comes after a long vowel.
Long vowel means ge.
Say the word: pay-j. Is the a short or long?
items.explanation: The a in page is a long vowel, so the /j/ sound is spelled ge.

items.prompt: Add -ing to swim and write the new word: ___
hints: Swim is a short word with a short vowel.
Short vowel then one consonant means double the last letter.
Look at the last letter of swim and the vowel before it.
items.explanation: For a short word with one short vowel and one final consonant, double the last letter before adding ing: swimming.

items.prompt: Which word is spelled correctly?

options.why: When a word ends in y after a consonant, y changes to i, but the n of ness stays.
The y should change to i before ness.
Ness has two s letters.

hints: The root word is happy.
When a word ends in consonant plus y, change y to i.
Then add ness.
items.explanation: The y changes to i before the suffix: happy becomes happiness.

items.prompt: Which word is spelled correctly?

options.why: When the suffix starts with a consonant, the silent e usually stays.
The suffix is spelled ment.
There is only one n at the start.

hints: The root word is manage and the suffix is ment.
Ment begins with a consonant.
Do we drop the e before a consonant suffix?
items.explanation: We keep the silent e before a suffix that starts with a consonant, so manage plus ment is management.

items.prompt: Add the suffix to each root word to complete the table.
head: Root word
Suffix
New word
hints: Check the ending of each root word.
Carry changes y to i. Stop doubles the p. Nice drops the e.
Hope keeps its e because ful starts with a consonant.
items.explanation: Carry becomes carried, stop doubles to stopping, nice drops the e to give nicer, and hope keeps its e in hopeful.

items.prompt: Match each root word and suffix to the correct spelling.
hints: Look at the last letters of each root word.
Y changes to i. Words ending in le lose the e. True loses its e before ly.
Start with easy: change the y to an i.
items.explanation: Easy and happy change y to i. Gentle loses le and takes ly. True drops its e. Basic needs ally to give basically.

items.prompt: Which word is spelled correctly?

options.why: The rule is: i before e, except after c.
The vowel pair is ei after c.
The word needs two vowels between c and v.

hints: Remember the rule i before e, except after c.
The letters before the ei pair are rec.
After c the letters swap to ei.
items.explanation: After the letter c, the pair is written ei. The word is receive.

items.prompt: The rule is: i before e, except after c. Choose the two words that are exceptions to this rule.

options.why: Receive follows the rule, because ei comes after c.
Field follows the rule: i comes before e.

hints: An exception breaks the rule.
Look for ei without a c before it.
Weird and one other have ei with no c.
items.explanation: Weird and seize have ei but no c before it, so they are exceptions. Receive and field follow the rule.

items.prompt: Which plural is an exception to the rule that f changes to ves?

options.why: Wolf follows the rule and becomes wolves.
Leaf follows the rule and becomes leaves.
Shelf follows the rule and becomes shelves.

hints: Many words ending in f change to ves in the plural.
Say the singular words: wolf, leaf, shelf, roof.
Which plural just adds s?
items.explanation: Roof is an exception: the plural is roofs. Wolf, leaf and shelf change f to ves.

items.prompt: Nina remembers how to spell necessary with the saying "one collar and two sleeves". What kind of spelling strategy is this?

options.why: She is using a saying, not the sounds of the word.
She is using her own memory aid.
The saying does not split the word into syllables.

hints: The saying helps her remember letters.
Collar and sleeves stand for c and s.
Look for the choice about a memory aid.
items.explanation: A mnemonic is a saying that helps you remember. Here it reminds her of one c and two s.

items.prompt: Match each spelling strategy to an example.
pairs: there is a rat in separate
one collar and two sleeves for necessary
hints: Each strategy has a different way of helping you.
Related words share a root. A hidden word sits inside the longer word.
Start with Feb-ru-ar-y: how is it split?
items.explanation: You can split a word into syllables, use a related word, spot a hidden word or make a memory sentence.

items.prompt: Bayu is not sure if sign has a g, so he thinks about signal. Which strategy is he using?

options.why: Sign does not sound like it has a g.
He is not using a saying.
He is not copying the word.

hints: Signal and sign share a root.
The g can be heard in signal.
Which strategy uses words from the same family?
items.explanation: The g is easy to hear in signal, and sign comes from the same family. This is a related word strategy.

items.prompt: Build the sentence.
hints: It is a short instruction.
It tells you how to say the word.
Start with Say.
items.explanation: Breaking a word into syllables is a good way to remember how to spell it.

items.prompt: A spellchecker does not underline "We went to there house." Why not?

options.why: The sentence uses the wrong word, there instead of their.

options.text: Because there is a real word, and the checker only checks whether words exist
Because spellcheckers only check capital letters
options.why: Spellcheckers check all words.
House is spelled correctly.

hints: A spellchecker compares words with a word list.
Is there a real word?
Does it check what the word means in the sentence?
items.explanation: Spellcheckers check that a word exists, not that it is the right one. You still need to proofread.

items.prompt: Put the steps for using a spelling log in order.
items: Notice a word you spelled wrongly
Check the correct spelling in a dictionary
Write the correct spelling in your log
Add a note about the tricky part
Test yourself on the word later
hints: First you must notice a mistake.
You need the right spelling before you can record it.
Testing yourself comes last.
items.explanation: You find the mistake, check it, record it, add a tip and test yourself later.

items.prompt: Which entry would be most helpful in a spelling log?

options.why: This only repeats the word without any help.
This does not say which word.

options.text: Wrong: seperate. Right: separate. Tip: there is a rat in separate.

options.why: This is a feeling and does not help you remember.

hints: A log should show what was wrong and what is right.
A tip helps you remember next time.
Look for the entry with the misspelling, the correct spelling and a tip.
items.explanation: A good entry shows the mistake, the correct spelling and a tip to remember it.
